title: South Korea's Kospi Swings From Bear Market to Recovery on AI Trade
excerpt: The benchmark index rebounded sharply after a 25% decline from June highs, with Temasek's reported interest in Samsung and SK Hynix and easing leveraged positions fueling renewed confidence.
body:
• South Korea's Kospi swung from a bear market to recovery in roughly a month, driven by renewed confidence in AI and semiconductor demand
  • Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which account for over half of the Kospi's market cap, have rebounded sharply after a 25% index decline from June highs
  • Reports of Singapore's Temasek planning investments in both chipmakers helped lift the Kospi 3.7% in a single session
  • JPMorgan analysts say leveraged ETF unwinding is "complete" and hedge fund deleveraging is roughly 90% done

South Korea's Kospi has staged one of the most dramatic turnarounds in recent market history, swinging from a bear market triggered by a semiconductor selloff to a sharp recovery in just over a month — propelled by renewed confidence in the artificial intelligence trade and fresh institutional buying interest.

The benchmark index plunged roughly 25% from its record closing high of 9,114.55 in late June, entering bear market territory in early July as investors took profits on chip stocks that had driven a historic rally. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix — which together account for more than half of the Kospi's market capitalization — dropped more than 6% in single sessions, triggering circuit breakers multiple times.

A Bear Market in the World's Best Performer

The selloff was jarring but came in the context of extraordinary gains. Even at its lowest point, the Kospi remained up roughly 60% for the year, far outpacing the S&P 500 and MSCI's broadest global equity gauge. SK Hynix had surged over 200% in 2026, while Samsung climbed more than 130%, fueled by explosive demand for memory chips powering AI applications.

"It's a wake-up call. Both for those who are greedy and those who are fearful. For those who were fearful, it's a great time to buy in."

— Francis Tan, Chief Strategist for Asia, Indosuez Wealth Management

The correction was amplified by single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds that launched in South Korea in May. These products turbocharged gains on the way up but exacerbated losses during the downturn. Citi estimated total retail investor losses in leveraged ETFs at approximately $38.7 billion, prompting a public apology from Finance Minister Koo Yun-cheol for allowing the products without adequate safeguards.

Temasek and Institutional Buying Signal Recovery

The recovery accelerated after Asia Business Daily reported that Temasek — Singapore's $400 billion state-owned investment company — was planning direct investments in both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The news sent Samsung shares up 6.7% and SK Hynix higher in Seoul, lifting the broader Kospi 3.7% in a single session.

A Temasek spokesperson told Barron's that the group did not seek advice from the Korean government on investment timing and noted that its interest in both companies was not new, without confirming or denying specific new investments.

JPMorgan analysts added to the bullish case, noting that leveraged ETF unwinding appeared "complete" and hedge fund deleveraging was roughly 90% finished. The bank cited historical data showing a median 12-month return of about 28% following previous emerging-market corrections of similar magnitude.

Structural Risks Remain

Despite the rebound, the Kospi's concentration risk remains elevated. Samsung and SK Hynix's combined weight in the index means sharp moves in either stock can overwhelm the broader market — a dynamic that Goldman Sachs analysts have warned could trigger forced selling by foreign investors hitting diversification thresholds.

Foreign investors have pulled a record of nearly $110 billion from South Korean equities this year, largely to rebalance portfolios after the market's surge in value. Domestic retail investors have carried much of the buying burden, often using margin loans.

"I don't like to buy markets that have been going straight up. I like things to be depressed and to have lots of unhappiness and gloom around."

— Jim Rogers, Co-founder of the Quantum Fund

The AI Cycle's Staying Power

The fundamental investment case for Korean chip stocks rests on the durability of AI-driven demand. Samsung recently projected a 19-fold surge in second-quarter operating profit, and both companies have pledged 800 trillion won ($518 billion) in new fab investments as part of a national semiconductor strategy.

Evercore analysts noted that the Korean memory chip price cycle has historically averaged about 1.8 years, with the most recent trough occurring in June 2025. That could mean peak earnings growth extends into the second or third quarter of 2027 — or even longer if the AI buildout mirrors the duration of the internet boom.

For now, the Kospi's wild ride underscores both the immense opportunity and the concentrated risk in betting on the AI semiconductor cycle through one of the world's most concentrated stock markets.
